activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Evan woke up early. Today was his big day. He was going to the dentist for the very first time. "I get to sit in a big chair!" he told his gray cat. He counted his teeth with his finger. "One, two, three, all the way to twenty!"

He packed his small pillow in a bag. He wanted to hug it in the car. Mom smiled and buckled him in. The seat clicked.

At the dentist, a kind lady waved. Evan looked at her hands. Her hands were blue! "Why are your hands blue?" he asked. The dentist held them up. "These are my gloves. I wear gloves when I put my fingers or tools in your mouth."

Evan touched one glove. It felt smooth and stretchy. The dentist pulled it and let go. Snap! Evan laughed out loud. He opened his mouth wide, just like a lion.

At home, Evan put his pillow on the couch. He snapped his own pretend gloves on his hands. "Open wide, cat!" he said. The cat yawned big.

story:

Kinsley found a book. She held it up. The bear on the page stood on his head. The words sat at the bottom of the sky. "Look, Milo!" she said. "The bear is upside down!" Milo came over and laughed.

Ms. Dlamini turned the book around. Now the words sat at the bottom of the page. The bear stood on his feet. Kinsley blinked. She turned the book upside down again. The bear stood on his head again. The words flew up to the top. "Funny bear," she said. She turned it back. The bear sat down. The words sat at the bottom, all in a row.

Kinsley put her finger on the row. "These are the words," she said. "They tell about the bear." Milo leaned in close. Kinsley turned to the first page. "This is the front," she said. She opened it and began. "Bear woke up. Bear saw pink flowers."

story:
Ryan sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. His tummy felt funny. "The shot might hurt," he told his mom. "Just a little pinch," said the nurse. "Then I have a surprise for you."

The nurse cleaned Ryan's arm with a cool, wet wipe. Ryan counted with his mom. "One, two, three." The pinch came. It was small, like a bug kiss. Then it was done.

Ryan saw the nurse open a small paper wrapper. She put a small bandage over the spot on his arm. The bandage had yellow stars on it. "A star bandage!" said Ryan. He could not stop looking at it. The spot felt better already.

Afterward, Mom took Ryan to the ice cream shop. Ryan got pink strawberry ice cream in a cup. It was cold and sweet on his tongue. A man at the next table waved. "Nice stars," he said. Ryan held up his arm to show him. "One, two, three, four, five stars," he counted.

Conner from school came in with his dad. Conner ran over to see. "I got a shot too," Conner said. He pulled up his sleeve. His bandage had blue dinosaurs on it. Ryan laughed. "Next time, I want dinosaurs," he said, and he took another big bite of ice cream.

Matthew held his dad's hand at the street festival. There were red lanterns everywhere. There was a big dragon made of paper. There was food and drums and so many people.

"Can we dance too?" Matthew asked.

"Watch first," said his dad.

The drums went boom, boom, boom. The dancers hopped and turned. The dragon spun around. Zavier from Matthew's class was dancing too! He held his mom's hand and hopped. Ms. Tang waved from the stage. "The music makes us dance!" she called.

Then the music stopped. The dancers stopped too. Everything was quiet and still.

The music started again. The dancers danced again!

"The music makes the dancing!" said Matthew. "That is how it works!"

"Yes!" said his dad. "Dancing goes with the music."

Matthew pulled his dad's hand. "Let's dance now!"

They hopped and turned. Matthew saw a spider web shine on a lantern, slippery with rain drops. He laughed and spun again.

Boom, boom, boom went the drums. Matthew went hop, hop, hop.

Eleanor hopped out of bed. She walked to the sink. She got her little toothbrush. Mama put the paste on it. Eleanor brushed up and down. She brushed the front and the back.

Eleanor rinsed the brush. She looked in the mirror. Her teeth were clean and shiny. She yawned a big yawn.

"Good night, Eleanor," Mama said.

"Good night, teeth," said Eleanor.

story:
Liam stood at the edge of the backyard pool. The water was blue and cool. His tummy felt funny. "I want to float," he said. "But what if I sink?"

Mr. Warsame stepped into the pool. "I will hold you," he said. "My hands go under your back. Now you can let go of me."

Liam lay back in the water. He felt Mr. Warsame's hands under his back, like a soft plastic mat. Liam opened his eyes. The sky was up there. A cloud looked like a big white dog. Was the water holding him too?

"I'm floating!" Liam said. "I'm not sinking!" Aanya clapped from the pool steps. "Next it's my turn," she said.

Then Mr. Warsame took one hand away. Liam did not sink. He did not go under. He just lay there, light as a leaf.

"Can you take your other hand away?" Liam asked. Mr. Warsame smiled and let both hands go. Liam floated all by himself. He saw the cloud drift by, slow and slow.

"Look at me, Aanya!" Liam called. Aanya kicked her legs in the water. "Can a cloud ride on the sky like that?" she asked.

"Maybe it can," Liam said. He lay still and watched it go.

Then a red ball rolled under the table. Leon ran to the far end of the kitchen. It was dark back there. He could not see Dad. Dad could not see him. Leon looked around the corner. No Dad. activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Matthew wanted to make something with him, something just theirs. In the kitchen, Grandpa got out a big bowl. "I will show you my special bread," he said. "My mother made it, and her mother made it too. Our family has made it for a long time."

Matthew poured the flour. Grandpa showed him how to mix and press the dough. Matthew pressed it flat, then folded it, then pressed again. It was soft and warm, like a cloud. They put the dough in the bowl and covered it with a towel. Then they had to wait. Matthew wanted to peek. "Not yet," said Grandpa, and they sat down to talk about the park instead.

After a long time, Grandpa lifted the towel. The dough was big now. Matthew's eyes went wide. His pressing had helped make it grow. Dad put the pan into the hot oven, and Matthew watched from far away. Soon the kitchen smelled warm and sweet.

The next day they took the bread to the park. Marion was there by the lion statue, and Ariel was on the swings. Matthew gave them each a piece. "My grandpa taught me," he said. "It is our family bread." Ariel took a bite and smiled. "Can I help next time?"

activity: making an art or craft project

Aaron sat in the backyard with his markers. He was drawing a big red truck on paper. Flynn sat next to him, drawing a sun.

Aaron reached for the blue marker. It slipped in his hand. The blue tip touched his skin. Now his hand had a blue stripe on it.

Aaron looked at the stripe. His lip began to wobble. "It won't come off," he said. He thought he might cry.

Mr. Goh was watering the flowers nearby. He came over and looked at Aaron's hand. "Let's try soap and water," he said. "These markers are washable. Washable means they wash off."

Aaron went to the outside tap. Mr. Goh put soap on his hand. Aaron rubbed and rubbed under the water. The blue stripe got smaller. Then it was gone. His hand was clean.

Aaron laughed. "It went away!" He ran back to Flynn. "Look, one stripe, two stripes, three stripes!" he said, drawing on his paper. "And if I get one on my hand, I can wash it off."

Flynn smiled and drew a big yellow snowman with a bumpy carrot nose. "The snowman has no snow," Flynn said.

"Then we will draw him some," said Aaron, and he picked up the white marker.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Kinsley sat at Grandma's big table. The bowls were full of corn. The corn was yellow and a little salty. Everyone held hands. It was time for the family blessing.

Kinsley did not know the blessing yet. She opened her mouth. Nothing came out. She looked down at her lap.

Grandma squeezed her hand. "Take your time," said Grandma. "We can wait." They all waited. The room was quiet and warm.

Kinsley thought about the corn. "Grandma, where did the corn grow?" she asked. "On a farm," said Grandma. "A farmer picked it for us."

Kinsley thought about that. The farmer had pulled the corn from the tall plants. Then the corn came all the way here. Kinsley took a big breath.

"Thank you for our food," she said. "Thank you for the corn. And thank you to the farmer." Grandma smiled wide. "That is a good blessing," she said. "It says thank you."

Then Grandma passed the bread. Kinsley took a warm piece and ate it all up. "Can I say it again tomorrow?" she asked. Grandma laughed and squeezed her hand one more time.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Rehmat stood by the pool in her red swimsuit. Today was game day! Ms. González held a big box. Inside were beanbags and a hoop. "First we throw," said Ms. González. "Then we catch. Then we jump in and drink our juice."

Rehmat grabbed a beanbag. She swung her arm high and let go. The beanbag flew way over the hoop. It landed near Marvin's feet. "Too far!" laughed Marvin. "One, two, three misses," counted Paige.

Ms. González picked up the beanbag. She held it low, near her knees. Her arm swung from down low, forward and up. The beanbag went up and dropped into the middle of the hoop. "Try that way," she said.

Rehmat held her beanbag down low. She counted, "One, two, three!" Her arm swung forward and up. The beanbag sailed through the air. Plunk! It landed in the hoop.

"You did it!" said Paige. "One, two, three baskets!" said Marvin. Now it was catch time. Paige threw the big beach ball. Rehmat opened both arms wide. She caught it and hugged it tight. The ball smelled like sunscreen and felt bumpy.

Then everyone jumped in the pool. The water was cool and splashy. Rehmat was so tired and happy. After juice, she yawned a big yawn. "You might fall asleep right here," said Ms. González. Rehmat laughed and hugged her wet beanbag. "More hoop tomorrow!"

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Alice wakes up in her soft, warm bed. The sun is bright at her window. She hears Dad making breakfast in the kitchen. "Eggs today," he says. Alice wants to help, but first she has a small problem. She needs to use the toilet.

Alice sits on the toilet. Then she pulls up her pants and runs to the kitchen. But wait. The toilet is still full. She forgot something! What did she forget? Alice runs back to look.

"First we flush," says Dad, following her. Alice presses the big silver handle. Whoosh! The water spins round and round. She watches it all go down. That was the first step. But there is one more step after that.

"Now we wash our hands," says Dad. He turns on the tap. Warm water runs over Alice's little hands. The soap is slippery and smells like flowers. One, two, three, four, five bubbles. She counts them all. Then she dries her hands on the blue towel.

Now her hands are clean. Now she can help Dad. Alice sits on her chair and cracks nothing, but she does open the egg box for him. "Nice work, Alice," says Dad. Alice smiles and eats her warm egg.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Audrey sat at the dinner table. The bright lamp made a warm circle of light. Her dad set down three bowls. One was for animals. One was for toys. One was for foods.

Audrey picked up a carrot. "Food," she said. She dropped it in the foods bowl. Then came a little cow from her farm set. "Animal," she said. Clunk. Then a soft toy dog. She held it near the animal bowl. Her dad waited. She squeezed its furry arm. It did not wiggle. It did not bark. It just sat in her hand.

"Not alive," said Audrey. She moved it over. "Toy dog." Clunk, into the toy bowl. Her dad smiled and swept the crumbs off the table with his hand.

"Now dinner," he said. Audrey put one strawberry in her own bowl. "Food," she said. She took a big bite.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Ethan stood at the school gate. His tummy felt funny, like little butterflies. His mom held his hand tight.

"My tummy feels fluttery," Ethan said.

Mom knelt down. "That means you feel nervous. It is okay to feel nervous on the first day of school. I felt nervous on my first day too."

"You did?" said Ethan.

"Yes! And then I saw my teacher and it got better."

Just then, a boy named Salem ran up to the gate. He was holding a special red truck. He rolled it on the ground and sent it right to Ethan's feet.

"Want to play trucks?" said Salem.

Ethan picked up the truck. The butterflies in his tummy flew away. Across the street, the school bell rang, warm and loud.

"Let's go together," said Salem.

Ethan smiled and took his new friend's hand. "Let's go!"

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Mya stood in the kitchen. Her tummy said it was breakfast time. She wanted toast with butter, all by herself. Her dad put two warm pieces of toast on her plate. Then he handed her the butter knife.

Mya dug the knife into the soft butter. She spread it across the toast, one, two, three strokes. The butter made shiny lines. Some spots were bare. She spread some more. Now the toast was covered, and it smelled yummy.

Next came the milk. Mya held the small cup. She poured the milk slowly, slowly. The milk rose up in the cup. Then her hand wiggled. A little white puddle sat on the table. Mya's lip went down at the corners.

She reached for the curly blue cloth. She wiped the puddle, one wipe, two wipes. The table was dry again. Mya poured one more time. This time her hand was steady. Not one drop spilled. She took a big bite of buttery toast and a big sip of milk. "I did it," said Mya, "all by myself."

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Aubrey sat in her seat in the family car. Click, click went her buckle. The car hummed under her feet. Today was shot day at the doctor. Aubrey did not like shot day. "I am afraid," she said.

Mom kept driving. "We will go together," said Mom. "I will be with you the whole time." Aubrey looked out the window. One tree, two trees, three trees went by. Then the car stopped. They were at the doctor's office.

In the office, Aubrey climbed on the big, high table. It felt cold and too big. Her legs swung in the air. The nurse came in with a little tray. Aubrey's eyes got wide. She started to cry.

"Come here," said Mom. Mom sat on a chair and pulled Aubrey onto her lap. Mom's arms went around her, warm like a blanket. Aubrey held Mom's hand. She squeezed it tight. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." The shot was done, that fast. It barely hurt at all.

They walked back to the car. The seat felt cozy now. The sun made a warm spot on her knee. "My turn for a sticker," said Aubrey. She stuck it right on her shirt and smiled.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
William loved the playroom floor. It had a big striped rug with squares on it. He wanted to build a house for his toy bear.

He found a round plate. "That is a circle," he said. He put it down for a wall. Then he found a tiny button. Mackenzie shook her head. "That can't be a circle," she said. "It is too small. The plate is a circle."

William held the button up. He looked at the plate. Then he looked at the button. Both went round and round, with no corners at all. "Look," he said. He spun the button on the floor. It rolled just like the plate rolled.

"Big circle, tiny circle," said Mackenzie. She clapped. They used the button for a little window. William found a triangle block for the roof. The bear had a house at last.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Beatrice came home from Grandma's house. She had a big blue bag. The trip was over now.

"Time to unpack," said her mama. Beatrice put her bag on the floor. She opened it up. Out came her shirt. Out came her soft bunny. Out came her little red shoes.

She tipped her shoe upside down. Sand fell out! Sand from the beach at Grandma's house. Beatrice laughed and laughed. The sand made a small pile on the rug.

"That is beach sand," said her mama. She helped sweep it up. Beatrice put her shirt in the drawer. She put her bunny on the bed. She put her shoes on the shelf. The bag was empty at last.

Beatrice smelled her shirt. It smelled like Grandma's flowers. Her feet felt funny without shoes, like something new.

"Unpack, unpack," sang Beatrice. She hugged her empty bag. "All done!"

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Wesley was at Grandma's house. He sat at the big table. Emmie sat next to him. They were painting pictures.

"One cat," said Wesley. "Two cats. Three cats." He painted three orange cats. Emmie painted three orange cats too. Grandma put the paintings in the sun to dry. The paint began to shine.

Then Wesley wanted his painting. But there were two papers. Both had three orange cats. "Which one is mine?" he asked. He looked and looked. He could not tell.

Emmie held up her paper. Her name was on it. Letters at the top said Emmie. "Look," she said. "I wrote my name." Wesley picked up a crayon. He wrote W-E-S on his paper. Now everyone knew which painting was his.

"How did you know?" he asked Emmie. "Grandma helped me," she said. Wesley smiled. He carried his cats to Grandma. "This one is mine," he said. "It says Wesley."

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Ryan went to the bank with his mom. It was cold outside. Ryan held his coat in his hands.

"I will put it on myself," Ryan said. He pushed one arm into a sleeve. Then he pushed his other arm in too. Both arms went into the same sleeve! The coat looked like one long tube. Ryan laughed and laughed. He waved his arms like a big flipper.

His mom smiled. "Try again," she said. Ryan shook the coat out. This time he looked at it. One arm went into one sleeve. The other arm went into the other sleeve. Each arm had its own sleeve. The coat sat just right on his shoulders.

Now the zipper. Ryan pulled it up, up, up. It stuck near the top. He pulled again, slow and steady. Click. The zipper closed all the way.

At the bank, the warm air felt good. Ryan patted his chest. "I did it," he said. "All by myself."

His mom said, "Next time, we can work on your hat."

"Maybe," said Ryan. "But the coat was my big dream today." He zipped it down and zipped it back up, just to hear the sound.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Eliana ran to her cubby at daycare. She touched the tag on it. The tag said "Eliana." "That is my name," she said.

Ms. Boateng held out a card. "This came for you today." The card was smooth and red. Eliana opened it. It was from Louie. The card said "Eliana" at the top.

Eliana looked at the cubby. Then she looked at the card. "Same!" she said. "The letters are the same." Ms. Boateng smiled. "Louie can spell your name."

Jane came over. "How do you spell it?" she asked. "E, L, I, A, N, A," said Eliana, pointing at each letter. The letters went in the same order both times.

Eliana turned the pages of the card, one by one, front to back. On the last page, there was a picture of bread. It was a picture of bread with a candle in it.

"Happy birthday, Eliana!" said Louie, running in the door.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Rosalie took the big road with her dad. They walked to the wide doors of the temple. Inside, Ms. Chaudhry was waiting with her drum.

"Hello, Rosalie," said Ms. Chaudhry. "Today we will clap and sing. You will meet the beat."

Ryan and Reese sat on the mats too. Ms. Chaudhry tapped the drum. Rosalie began to sing right away. But Ryan and Reese did not sing yet. Rosalie sang all alone. She stopped and her face felt warm.

"Wait for the count," said Ms. Chaudhry, kindly. "I will say one, two, three, four. Then we all start singing together."

Ms. Chaudhry lifted her hand. "One, two, three, four." Ryan and Reese began to sing. Rosalie began too, right on four. Now they all sang at the same time.

Then they clapped. Ms. Chaudhry tapped the drum, boom, boom, boom. Rosalie clapped her hands on each boom. She saw that when her hand went down, the drum went boom. Clap, boom. Clap, boom.

They sang "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star." Rosalie knew all the words. She did not look at anyone. She sang them all by herself.

"Again!" said Rosalie.

Ms. Chaudhry smiled and lifted her hand. "One, two, three, four."

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Aiden was busy in the playroom. He wanted his red ball. He looked under the little chair. He looked behind the big plant. "Where is my ball?" he asked. His dad said, "Look in the toy box."

The toy box was full of everything. Blocks were on the floor. A doll was on the rug. The ball was under the teddy bear. Aiden put a block in the box. The box had one less thing on the floor. He put in another block. Now the floor had more room.

Aiden held up the doll. "Doll goes in," he said. Dad said, "Yes, it does. Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys." Aiden smiled. He put the doll in. He picked up the ball. "Ball goes in too!" he said.

Then Aiden wanted to make a picture. Dad got the glue and some paper. Aiden spread the glue with a stick. He stuck on a red circle. He pressed it down. The paper was heavy with glue, so it sank down flat on the table. Aiden held his ball up high. "My ball can sit here," he said, and he set it right on top of the full toy box.
